why: Briefing states flatly that no harness distinguishes a wedged agent from a productive one - both keep emitting - so detecting thrash means watching one pane over time and remembering what it did five minutes ago, across 3-12 sessions. Impact is loss-prevention: an unnoticed loop burns quota and hours, which is the 76-100 band.

Ranking sessions by who needs you most requires the cross-session view the briefing says does not exist ("No harness displays anything about sessions other than the one in front of you"), so the user must cycle every pane and hold the ordering in their head. Impact changes a real triage decision many times a day but rarely prevents concrete loss on its own.

A raw count is the one cross-session fact that is nearly free: the terminal tab bar shows it, and the briefing lists tmux list-panes/list-windows as an unaided move. Deciding which are actually *active* costs more, but the count itself is one command away. The item itself records no decision attached, so impact is interesting-only.

An action, and one the briefing does not cover - it lists Spacedock stage strips only as something Cargento derives. By hand, promoting a running ad-hoc session into a managed workflow means reconstructing its state and scaffolding the workflow manually, which is real work rather than a command. Impact is a workflow convenience for the subset of users who run workflows at all.

The briefing lists ps as an unaided move, and a crashed session usually leaves a visible pane, so for one session this is cheap. The cost is that you only look after you already waited - across 3-12 panes the death is silent until you cycle to it. Impact is real: waiting on a dead session is pure wasted wall-clock, and restarting is a concrete action.

Claude Code has /usage reporting quota, one command away, but the briefing does not say it breaks quota out per model, and Barista is described as caching 5-hour and weekly percentages only. So the Opus-vs-Sonnet split is at best one command plus inference, and absent on every other harness. Impact is high: it converts a hard stop into a model switch.

Two things the briefing says nothing surfaces have to combine: quota is shown only as a current figure with no burn rate projected forward, and no harness writes a hand-off. Anticipating the wall and authoring a clean continuation prompt before it hits is effectively unobtainable by hand. Impact prevents the concrete loss of a half-finished session dying mid-task.

Rate over time needs history, and the briefing says no harness retains queryable history across sessions, nor projects any rate. Reconstructing a sparkline means parsing session files on disk repeatedly - a script a normal user would not write. But the item carries no decision attached, so instant access changes nothing the user does; it is ambience.

Both halves are individually reachable - the plan is scrollback in the pane, and git status is on the briefing list of unaided moves - but comparing them is manual correlation across several places, repeated per session. Impact changes a real steering decision regularly: silent scope drift caught late is rework, caught early is one sentence of correction.

Scored cross-harness. The briefing is explicit that a blocked prompt is fully on screen in its own pane, and Claude Desktop even shows per-session dots, but no harness shows it for any session other than the one in front of you - so with 3-12 panes the user must poll, and reliability is the failure mode, not reachability. Impact is the top band: an unnoticed block is an idle agent and a stalled human.
